walkthroughs.body_html:
Religious & Ethical Teachings about Relationships — a core area of GCSE Religious Studies.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Religious & Ethical Teachings about Relationships brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Religious & Ethical Teachings about Relationships.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Which encyclical banned Catholic contraception in 1968?
options: Humanae Vitae
Rerum Novarum
Pacem in Terris
Laudato Si

mcqs.q: What is the maximum number of wives in Islam?
What is the problem of evil?
options: It is the question of whether evil people will go to hell.
Jesus was a human who became God after his resurrection.
If God is all-loving, all-knowing and all-powerful, why does evil and suffering exist? Logically, all four cannot be true together without explanation.
It is the question of whether the devil really exists.
Hinduism worships no gods, only ancestors.
Jesus was a human who became God after his resurrection.
It is more accurately described as henotheistic or monistic — many gods (devas) are considered aspects or manifestations of one ultimate reality (Brahman).
Hinduism is straightforwardly polytheistic with millions of separate gods.

mcqs.q: What do orthodox Christians believe about the nature of Jesus?
options: He is fully God and fully human at the same time (the incarnation) — both natures united in one person, as defined at the Council of Chalcedon.
It is the question of whether the devil really exists.
Jesus was half God and half human.
Jesus was a human who became God after his resurrection.
